name: Gawar-Bati
confidence_why: Liljegren and Soan's 2025 instrumental study finds default final-syllable stress (the only pattern in uninflected nouns, with stress staying on the root under case inflection), and the sole dissent is Morgenstierne's 1950 sketch, which reported only "great confusion of stress" among its three informants and declined to state any rule.

catalog_quote: No relevant tones were observed. There is great confusion of stress (e. g. 1 m'usa: 3 muṣ'a, 1 'ānda: 3 ānd'a), and it is not possible to lay down any rules regarding its place. Note, however, 1,3 b'uṛa grandfather; buṛ'a deaf.

new_statements.quote: Stress is only partly contrastive in Gawarbati. The most frequent stress pattern is one with main stress on the final syllable. This is also the only stress pattern found as far as uninflected nouns are concerned. It is, however, possible to find minimal pairs exemplifying stress contrasts if we compare words across inflectional paradigms [...] The disyllabic item /ˈgələ/ 'into the valley' is a case-inflected form of the noun /gəl/ 'valley'. In the inflected form of the word, stress remains on the root, i.e., on its first syllable. This contrasts with the item /gəˈlə/ 'hill', a non-inflected disyllabic noun, with its "default" stress on its final, in this case second, syllable.

Adds acoustic correlates (F0 > duration; intensity not significant).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default main stress on the final syllable of the word; this is the only pattern in uninflected nouns. Stress is fixed to the root: when an inflectional suffix is added the stress stays where it was in the root (so a suffixed disyllable is initially stressed), which yields surface minimal pairs like /ˈgələ/ 'into the valley' vs /gəˈlə/ 'hill'. Stress is therefore only partly contrastive; acoustic correlates are higher F0 and, less so, longer duration, with intensity not significant.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; the paper only measures main stress (53 disyllables with final stress; preliminary trisyllables show the same tendency). It notes that 'systematic measurements of non-final stressed syllables vis-a-vis final non-stressed syllables have not been carried out' (p. 147).
new_statements.exceptions: Inflected forms keep root stress rather than shifting to the new final syllable (/ˈgələ/ 'into the valley', /ˈdəntə/ 'in the tooth', /ˈmalə/ 'herd OBL' vs uninflected /gəˈlə/ 'hill', /dənˈtə/ 'ridge', /maˈlə/ 'down below'). Also p. 145: /e/ and /i/ 'may be neutralized in some environments, e.g., in unstressed positions and in open final syllables'.
new_statements.identity_note: Liljegren & Soan 2025 describe primarily the Arandu (Haranu) variety in Lower Chitral, Pakistan (speakers AS, FA, NU), with comparisons to the Nari (Afghanistan) variety (speakers AG, FH); the stress measurements come from speakers NU and AS, i.e. the Pakistani Arandu variety. Kohistani 1993 covers 'Gawarbati' without a stated variety (record only).

audit.recode_to: Fixed final (default word-final stress; the only pattern in uninflected nouns), with morphologically conditioned non-final stress: case/inflectional suffixes do not take stress, so inflected forms keep stress on the root (/ˈgələ/ 'valley-LOC' vs /gəˈlə/ 'hill'), making stress 'only partly contrastive' on the surface. Deciding source: Liljegren & Soan 2025, JIPA 55:146-147. Keep Morgenstierne 1950:9 as a historical note (inter-informant variation; b'uṛa vs buṛ'a pair).
